summary: Describes a way for a TLS server to resume sessions without keeping per-client state. The server packs the session state into an encrypted ticket and hands it to the client, which presents it later to resume. It obsoletes RFC 4507 and was itself replaced by RFC 8446 and RFC 9846.

eli5.summary: Instead of the shop remembering you, it gives you a sealed note to bring back next time. That saves the shop from keeping files on every customer.

questions: how does tls session resumption work
what is in a tls session ticket
subtitle: The server seals the session state into a ticket and hands it to the client, so it does not have to remember anyone.

tldr.problem: A TLS server that resumes sessions normally has to keep per-client session state, which is costly for servers with many users, long caches, load balancing or little memory.
tldr.mechanism: The server encrypts and integrity-protects the session state into a ticket using a key only it knows, sends it in a NewSessionTicket handshake message, and the client later presents it in a SessionTicket extension in the ClientHello.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5077 obsoleted RFC 4507 to fix an encoding error, and it has since been replaced by RFC 8446 and RFC 9846.

today: RFC 5077 is obsoleted by RFC 8446 and RFC 9846, and it was updated by RFC 8447. It obsoleted RFC 4507.

sections.title: Resuming TLS Without Server State
sections.content:
This RFC defines a way to resume a TLS session without session-specific state at the server. It works with any ciphersuite and applies to TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346). It builds on the TLS extensions of RFC 4366 and adds one new message type.

The RFC lists four situations where this helps: servers that handle many transactions from different users, servers that want to cache sessions for a long time, the ability to load balance requests across servers, and embedded servers with little memory.

The term ticket means a cryptographically protected data structure that the server creates and later consumes to rebuild session state. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4507 to correct an encoding error that made that specification differ from deployed implementations.
sections.eli5: The server does not have to keep a notebook about every visitor. It writes the notes on a locked slip and lets the visitor carry it.

sections.title: How Tickets Are Issued and Used
sections.content:
A client signals support by including a SessionTicket extension in its ClientHello. The extension is empty if the client has no ticket yet. If the server wants to use the mechanism, it replies with an empty SessionTicket extension in the ServerHello and later sends a NewSessionTicket handshake message, before the ChangeCipherSpec and after verifying the client's Finished message. The ticket holds session state such as the ciphersuite and master secret, encrypted and integrity-protected with a key known only to the server.

The client caches the ticket with the master secret and other parameters. To resume, it puts the ticket in the SessionTicket extension of the ClientHello. The server decrypts it, checks it, and resumes using the state inside. On success it may also renew the ticket. If the server cannot or does not want to honor the ticket, it falls back to a full handshake, and it may still issue a new ticket afterwards. If a ticket is accepted but the handshake fails, the client SHOULD delete the ticket.

The client MUST NOT treat a new ticket as valid until it has verified the server's Finished message, and the server MUST NOT assume the client received an updated ticket until it verifies the client's Finished message.
sections.eli5: The first visit gives you a sealed note. Next time you show the note and skip the long chat. If the note does not work, you just do the long chat again.

sections.title: The Extension and the NewSessionTicket Message
sections.content:
The SessionTicket extension has been assigned the number 35, and its extension_data holds the ticket. A client with no ticket that can accept one MUST send a zero-length ticket. A client that cannot accept one MUST NOT include the extension, unless it is sending a non-empty ticket obtained by some other means. The server MUST send the extension in the ServerHello if it wishes to issue a ticket, and MUST NOT send it if it did not receive one.

The NewSessionTicket handshake message has been assigned the number 4. It carries a ticket_lifetime_hint, a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order giving seconds relative to when the ticket is received, and the opaque ticket. A value of zero means the lifetime is unspecified. The client SHOULD delete the ticket when the time expires, and a server MAY treat a ticket as valid for a shorter or longer time than the hint. The message is included in the hash used for the Finished messages.

For the Session ID, a server planning to issue a ticket SHOULD send an empty one. If the client presents a ticket and a non-empty Session ID, an accepting server MUST echo that same Session ID, which lets the client tell resumption from a full handshake.
sections.eli5: The note comes with a label that says how long to keep it. The label is only a hint, so the shop may accept it for a shorter or longer time.

sections.title: The Recommended Ticket Format
sections.content:
The ticket is opaque to the client, so its structure does not affect interoperability and implementations may diverge, as long as they take security seriously. Clients MUST NOT examine the ticket assuming it follows this document.

The recommended design uses two server keys: a 128-bit key for AES in CBC mode and a 256-bit key for HMAC-SHA-256. The ticket is made of a 16-byte key_name that identifies the key set, a 16-byte iv, the encrypted_state, and a 32-byte mac computed over the key name, IV, the 2-octet length of the encrypted state and the state itself.

The encrypted state is a StatePlaintext holding the protocol version, ciphersuite, compression method, a 48-byte master secret, a ClientIdentity and a timestamp used to expire tickets. The identity type is anonymous, certificate-based or pre-shared key.
sections.eli5: The sealed note has a label saying which lock was used, a scrambled message, and a stamp that shows nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tickets must be authenticated and encrypted to prevent modification or eavesdropping. A stolen ticket does not help an attacker resume a session because it is encrypted and the attacker lacks the key, but the server MUST use strong encryption and integrity protection. A forged or altered ticket is not possible if a strong integrity algorithm such as keyed HMAC-SHA-256 is used.

The key_name lets a server cheaply reject tickets it did not issue, and verification should be lightweight to limit denial of service. For keys, the RFC recommends secure generation, at least 128 bits of strength, no other use, regular changes, and a change if the format or algorithms change. The server controls ticket lifetime, which may be longer than the 24-hour lifetime recommended in RFC 4346.

On privacy, ticket contents are confidentiality protected, but an on-path observer who sees the same ticket in multiple handshakes may link them, so unlinkability is not necessarily provided.
sections.eli5: A stolen note is useless without the shop's key, but if you wave the same note around many times, someone watching can tell it is the same visitor.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4507
sections.content:
RFC 4507 had an encoding error that produced two length fields, one for the extension contents and one for the ticket. The RFC removes the redundant field to match what implementations actually send. For a 256-byte ticket, the extension is now type 35, a length of 256 for the ticket, then the ticket. The RFC states there were no known implementations that followed the old encoding.

The encoding of an empty extension was ambiguous in RFC 4507. Servers wanting to support old clients should answer an empty extension encoded the same way as received. Other clarifications cover issuing no new ticket on resumption, the lifetime being relative to receipt, the NewSessionTicket message being in the Finished hash, the Session ID interaction, a recommendation of SHA-256, and extra data in StatePlaintext.
sections.eli5: The first edition printed the length twice by mistake. This version fixes it to match how everyone was already doing it.
